title: Ignatius to Polycarp
subtitle: a prisoner's advice to a young overseer: stand like an anvil, carry everyone
lead: The only one of Ignatius's seven letters written to one person: Polycarp, overseer of the church at Smyrna, who had received him on his way to die in Rome. From Troas, about to sail, Ignatius sends him a stream of short commands: 'Carry everyone, as the Lord carries you' (1:2), 'The same plaster does not heal every wound' (2:1), 'Stand firm like a struck anvil' (3:1). He tells him to care for widows, not to look down on slaves, and to see that 'men and women who marry should make their union with the overseer's approval' (4:1-5:2).

Then he turns to the whole church as an army: 'Let your baptism remain as your weapons, your faith as a helmet, your love as a spear' (6:2), with Latin soldiers' words for deserter, deposits and back pay. Polycarp is to choose 'God's runner' for Syria and to write to the churches ahead (7:2-8:1). No church counts the letter as Scripture; it is read here as an early witness, with the New Testament as the measure.
facts: No church. It is not in the New Testament of the Council of Trent (Catholic), the Westminster Confession (Reformed), the Second London Baptist Confession, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of 35 New Testament books, or the Thirty-Nine Articles' 'Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'.
Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, on his way to execution in Rome. Eusebius names the letter (Church History 3.36.10).

Written at Troas (8:1), with Ignatius to the Philadelphians and Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, after the letters from Smyrna (Eusebius, Church History 3.36.5-10). Lake: Eusebius's Chronicle puts the martyrdom 'in the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.', and there is 'a general tendency to think that Ignatius was really a martyr in Rome in the time of Trajan (98-117 A.D.)'.

Polycarp, overseer of the church at Smyrna (1:0), and through him the church (6:1)

Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1912), the short (middle) recension: the Medicean manuscript at Florence (G), the long recension (g), and the Latin (L), Armenian (A) and Syriac (S) versions, the Syriac including Cureton's abridgment.
authorship: The letter claims to be by 'Ignatius, also called Theophorus' (1:0), writing from Troas (8:1). Eusebius names it: from Troas Ignatius wrote 'in particular to Polycarp, who led' the church of Smyrna (Church History 3.36.10, the site's translation of the Greek). Polycarp's own letter to the Philippians speaks of 'the letters of Ignatius, the ones he sent us' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2), and Lightfoot takes these to be this letter and the one to the Smyrnaeans.

The seven letters survive in three forms: a long recension of thirteen letters with interpolations, the short recension of the seven Eusebius names, and a Syriac abridgment of three, Ephesians, Romans and this letter, found by Cureton in 1845 (Lake). In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia judged that 'the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius'. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again. Sergio Zañartu's survey (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), who argued that the short recension was made from the long one; R. Joly (1979), who held the letters a forgery written in Smyrna between 165 and 168; J. Rius-Camps (1980), who kept as genuine only the four letters written from Smyrna, so not this one; R. M. Hübner (1997), who dated the letters between 165 and 175; and T. Lechner (1999). Zañartu quotes W. R. Schoedel (1987), who expected the short recension to remain what 'the scholarly consensus today' sees in it, 'a collection of genuine letters of Bishop Ignatius of Antioch', and himself holds to its authenticity 'until the contrary is proved' (the site's translations of his Spanish). B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment. Lake follows the short recension.

audience.to: Polycarp, overseer of the church at Smyrna, a port of the Roman province of Asia, who had received Ignatius during his stay there (Lightfoot); and through him the Smyrnaean church, addressed directly in chapter 6. The church had widows in its care (4:1), slaves among its members (4:3), married people and some who stayed single (5:1-2), elders and deacons (6:1), and teachers who 'seem trustworthy but teach something different' (3:1).
audience.why: To encourage a church leader whom Ignatius admired and to set out his duties, and to put him in charge of a task Ignatius could not finish: since his guards were sailing suddenly, Polycarp was to call a council, elect an envoy to Antioch, and write to the churches ahead (7:1-8:1). Lightfoot: 'Like the Pastoral Epistles of S. Paul ... this letter is the exhortation of an older servant of Christ to a younger friend', and 'though special, it is not private'. Knowing this explains the change from 'you' singular to 'you' plural.
views: Lake: 'Modern English obscures the fact that this "you" is plural. The others are singular' (8:1), and the mix 'is very strange'. Lightfoot holds that from 6:1 Ignatius addresses the whole church and names Polycarp when he means him alone.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a source: Polycarp of Smyrna and what the other writings say of him, the letter to a person that turns to the church, the journey from Troas to Neapolis, the Latin army words, and the people greeted.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Reads the letter beside the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy 4-6; 2 Timothy 2), with Ephesians 4:2, Matthew 8:17 and 10:16, Ephesians 5:25, Ephesians 6:13-17, 1 Corinthians 7 and Philemon in the site's wording.

lenses.name: Church order and the churches
lenses.desc: Reads the letter for what it asks of a church leader: care of widows, slaves and the married (4-5), more frequent gatherings (4:2), the single life and marriage with the overseer's approval (5:2), and a council that elects an envoy (7:2).

sections.h: A letter to one man, and to his church
sections.b: Ignatius had stayed at Smyrna and come to admire its overseer (Lightfoot). From Troas he wrote to the Smyrnaean church and to Polycarp himself (Eusebius, Church History 3.36.10). Chapters 1-5 speak to Polycarp in the singular. At 6:1 the 'you' becomes plural and the church is addressed directly; 7-8 move between the two. Lightfoot: the letter 'was obviously intended to be communicated to the Smyrnæan Church'.

Most of the letter is short commands to a church leader: patience, prayer, care for each person by name (1:2-3), gentleness with the troublesome (2:1), firmness against false teachers (3:1). Then particular people: widows, whom the overseer must guard 'after the Lord' (4:1); slaves, who must not be despised nor long to be freed 'from the common fund' (4:3); husbands and wives; those who remain single, who must not boast; and those who marry, who should do so 'with the overseer's approval' (5:1-2). The views notes and deep notes at chapters 4 and 5 set out what the verses say and how they are read.

Ignatius pictures Polycarp as an athlete: 'a perfect athlete' (1:3), 'God's athlete' whose prize is incorruption (2:3), the one who 'takes the blows and wins' (3:1). Lake: 'athlete' was 'a favourite name for Christians who strove to excel in virtue'. To the church he speaks as to soldiers: pay, desertion, arms, helmet, spear, full armor, deposits and back pay (6:2), with three Latin army words.

sections.h: The messenger to Syria and Polycarp's own letter
sections.b: Ignatius asks Polycarp to call a council and elect 'God's runner' for Syria (7:2), and to write to the churches ahead because Ignatius is sailing suddenly for Neapolis (8:1). Polycarp's letter to the Philippians shows the request reached Philippi too: 'You wrote to me, both you and Ignatius, asking that if anyone goes to Syria, he should carry the letter from you as well' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1), and he sent them 'the letters of Ignatius, the ones he sent us, and the others we had here with us' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2).

spec.title: Claude's theory: the advice Polycarp kept
spec.body: Ignatius told Polycarp to 'preach about' the evil arts (5:1), to care for widows (4:1), and to stand firm under blows (3:1). Polycarp's own letter to the Philippians, which asks for news of Ignatius and those with him (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2), warns against false teachers, gives counsel for widows, and urges endurance, pointing to Ignatius as an example (Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1). I suggest that some of Polycarp's counsel may echo what Ignatius had written to him. This is my suggestion; Polycarp's letter does not quote this one, and both men drew on the same Pastoral Letters.
spec.refs: 3:1; 4:1; 5:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2

canon.summary: Ignatius to Polycarp is an early Christian letter in no church's Bible. Its author, the martyr Ignatius of Antioch, is honored as a saint by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches; its recipient is Polycarp of Smyrna.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books (1546) does not include it. The U.S. bishops' daily readings for 17 October 2026 are headed 'Memorial of Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Bishop and Martyr'.

The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bishop of Antioch' on 20 December; its life of him says he 'also addressed a letter to Saint Polycarp, who mentions a collection of the letters of Saint Ignatius in his letter to the Philippians (Ch. 13)'.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books, which adds eight books to the 27, among them 'The book of Clement' and the 'Didascalia', does not name it.
Not Scripture: Article VI receives 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'.

The calendar of the synod's Southern District commemorates 'Ignatius of Antioch, Pastor and Martyr' on 17 October; its page says that on his way to Rome he wrote to churches 'and also to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna'. That is a district page, not a statement of the synod.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as 'all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these'.
Not Scripture: the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 books, 'All of which are given by the inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life'.

provenance.b: Written at Troas as Ignatius's guards prepared to sail suddenly for Neapolis (8:1). Eusebius: from Troas he wrote 'in particular to Polycarp' (Church History 3.36.10). Polycarp kept the letter and sent copies of Ignatius's letters to Philippi (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2).

In the Greek Medicean manuscript at Florence (G) with the other short-recension letters except Romans; in the long recension (g); in Grosseteste's Latin of 1250 (L); in the Armenian (A), made from a lost Syriac; and in Syriac, including the abridgment of three letters (Ephesians, Romans and this one) that Cureton found in 1845 and Lightfoot and others showed 'to be merely an abridgment from a Syriac text of the short recension' (Lake).

rejected_why.h: A bishop's letter, not an apostle's
rejected_why.b: The early church received into the New Testament writings it held to come from the apostles and their circle. Ignatius sets himself below the apostles: 'They were apostles; I am a condemned man' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3).

rejected_why.h: Treated as a letter of a church writer
rejected_why.b: Eusebius names the letter in his history (Church History 3.36.10) and does not mention Ignatius in his survey of the books accepted, disputed and rejected for the New Testament (Church History 3.25). Polycarp, who received it, sent it on with the others as letters from which 'you will be able to gain a great deal' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2), not as Scripture.

cited_in.b: Jesus's 'sharp like snakes and pure like doves', put in the singular for one man (Lake's margin). The New Testament does not quote this letter.
Lightfoot: the armor 'was doubtless suggested by Ephes. vi. 13-17, which it closely resembles, though the parts of the armour are differently assigned'.
'Carried our diseases' (Lake's margin) behind 'Carry everyone's diseases'.
The soldier who pleases the one who enlisted him (Lake's margin); Lightfoot compares the whole letter with the Pastoral Letters.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to church life early in the second century the letter is of great value: it shows what was asked of a city's overseer (care for widows, slaves, the married and the single, frequent gatherings, firmness against false teaching) and how churches sent envoys to each other. Its text rests on one Greek manuscript of the short recension, the long recension and the versions, with Cureton's Syriac abridgment as a further witness. Lightfoot notes that, having little about heresy, it 'escaped with comparatively few changes' from the interpolator. Its historical claims fit Eusebius and Polycarp's own letter. In doctrine it follows the New Testament; its rule that marriages be made with the overseer's approval goes beyond it.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to early Christian belief
sections.b: High. The letter shows an overseer as pastor of every group in his church (1-5), a church called to obey its overseer, elders and deacons and to work 'together' (6:1), Christ confessed as timeless and invisible yet suffering 'for our sake' (3:2), baptism as the believer's armor (6:2), and a council electing an envoy (7:2).

The short recension survives in Greek in the Medicean manuscript (G); the long recension (g), the Latin (L) and the Armenian (A) correct its slips, and for this letter the Syriac abridgment adds a witness (Lake). Lightfoot's apparatus shows G reversing 'the Lord's flesh' at 5:2, reading 'God' for 'the Lord' at 5:2, dropping 'with you' at 6:2 and reading 'sufferer' for 'disciple' at 7:1; Lake prints the other witnesses there, and the variants give both. At 6:2 Syriac and Armenian witnesses have 'faith' as the arms and 'hope' as the helmet. Lake calls 2:3 'hopelessly obscure' in its details and 8:1's mix of singular and plural 'very strange'.

The letter claims to be by Ignatius at Troas, about to sail for Neapolis (8:1), writing to Polycarp. Eusebius knew it (Church History 3.36.10), and Polycarp's letter to the Philippians speaks of Ignatius's letter and of the plan to send to Syria (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1-2). The debate over the genuineness of the seven letters is in the authorship section; Rius-Camps (1980), as Zañartu reports him, did not count this letter among the genuine ones.

Matches: patience 'in love' (1:2; Ephesians 4:2); carrying others' burdens and diseases (1:2-3; Galatians 6:2; Matthew 8:17); 'sharp like snakes and pure like doves' (2:2; Matthew 10:16); care for widows (4:1; 1 Timothy 5:3-16); counsel to slaves (4:3; 1 Corinthians 7:21-23; 1 Timothy 6:1-2); husbands to love their wives as Christ the church (5:1; Ephesians 5:25); the single life as a gift without pride (5:2; 1 Corinthians 7:7); the armor of faith and love (6:2; Ephesians 6:13-17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8). Goes beyond: that marriages be made 'with the overseer's approval' and that the single person's purpose be known to the overseer (5:2) have no parallel in the New Testament, which says only 'in the Lord' (1 Corinthians 7:39); the rule that nothing be done without the overseer (4:1) goes beyond the Pastoral Letters. Conflicts: none on a point of doctrine.

how_to_read.b: Read it as Lightfoot suggests, like 1 and 2 Timothy: an older servant of Christ writing to a younger leader, with the church listening in.
Chapters 1-5 speak to Polycarp, chapter 6 to the church; in 7-8 Polycarp is named when he alone is meant.
Polycarp to the Philippians, on this site, shows the man who received this letter, his care for the churches and the plan to send to Syria (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1-2).
